ONEWALLET — Full reference for LLMs
====================================

Source: https://onewallet.store/
Whitepaper: https://onewallet.store/whitepaper.html
Version: v1.0 · May 2026 · Official Release · Approved by Product, Security, Legal, and Partnerships
Disclaimer: Forward-looking statements remain subject to product, security, and legal review. Not financial, legal, tax, or investment advice.

SECTION 1 — What ONEWALLET is
------------------------------
ONEWALLET is a Telegram-native Web3 wallet and payment rail. It bundles keyless Multi-Share custody, QR payments, merchant tools, and $1 utility into a single Telegram Mini App flow. Users open ONEWALLET inside Telegram, verify the device, create the wallet, and then send, pay, or earn from the Mini App. The default flow avoids app-store downloads and seed-phrase setup.

SECTION 2 — Custody and security model
---------------------------------------
ONEWALLET targets a 2-of-3 Shamir custody model across three shares: a device share, a Telegram-account-bound share, and a recovery share. Any single share alone — including the Telegram share — cannot reconstruct the key or sign a transaction. Any two of the three are combined on the user device in an isolated context to reconstruct the key, sign, then wipe it. Shares are rotatable.

Trust boundaries:
- Edge services see signing requests but never the complete key material.
- Each holder stores only one Shamir share and cannot sign unilaterally.
- Settlement broadcasts only after a valid signature returns.

Threat model (selected):
- Device theft → loss of one share → rotate device share via server + recovery cooperation.
- Telegram account or session hijack → the Telegram share alone cannot reconstruct the key or sign; an attacker still needs a second share (device or recovery); high-value transfers add re-auth and cooldown.
- Signing from a compromised device → malware on the device attempts to combine two shares; per-signature biometric re-auth, value caps, cooldowns, and anomaly checks raise attacker cost and surface intervention before high-value broadcasts.
- Coerced recovery attempt → user tricked or pressured into using the recovery share; time-locked recovery window with multi-step confirmation surfaces alerts before any share is released.

Custody isolation and hardware-protected key storage are described as target architecture, not a present-day guarantee. No custody model is unbreakable.

SECTION 3 — Recovery and seed phrases
--------------------------------------
ONEWALLET uses Multi-Share (Shamir) custody, so there is no single seed phrase a normal user must hold. If a user loses their device or Telegram account, recovery is designed around issuing a fresh device share and validating it through the recovery share. Losing a device or Telegram session does not give the Telegram share enough authority to move funds alone — a second share is still required. Advanced backup or export behavior remains subject to product and security approval.

SECTION 4 — Networks
---------------------
The public draft targets TON, Ethereum, BNB Chain, TRON, and major stablecoins (USDT, USDC, etc.). The final supported network list will be confirmed before public launch.

SECTION 5 — Merchant payments
------------------------------
Merchant flow: a merchant generates a QR invoice; the user scans it inside Telegram; ONEWALLET previews receiver, fees, and FX; Shamir signing completes the transaction; a settlement webhook supports POS reconciliation. Merchant tooling includes QR invoicing, stablecoin settlement, webhooks, and ecosystem rewards.

SECTION 6 — Fees and $1 utility
--------------------------------
Fees consist of network gas plus transparent ONEWALLET fees on swaps and merchant payments. Holding $1 is described as a way to reduce fees at preferential rates, subject to final token and legal review.

$1 token utility (positioning, not promises):
- Fee discount — holding $1 reduces payment and swap fees. (Designed)
- User rewards — earn $1 for payments and referrals. (Designed)
- Merchant incentives — $1 top-up lowers acceptance fees. (Designed)
- Ecosystem access — premium mini-apps. (Planned)
- Governance signal — vote on rewards and fees. (Planned)

ONEWALLET makes no price, return, or exchange-listing promises. $1 is positioned as a utility token.

SECTION 7 — Roadmap
--------------------
- Phase 1 — Core wallet (Multi-Share custody, TMA, multi-chain): completed.
- Phase 2 — Payments rail (QR invoices, settlement webhooks): in progress.
- Phase 3 — $1 utility (fee discount layer, reward engine): planned.
- Phase 4 — Ecosystem (mini-app store, partner program): planned.

Dates are intentionally omitted until owners approve public commitments.

SECTION 8 — Risks (disclosed)
------------------------------
- Custody compromise (high) — Shamir reconstructs the key at signing time, creating a brief on-device in-memory exposure window; a flaw in share rotation, reconstruction, or key wipe could expose funds.
- Platform dependency (high) — Telegram is the runtime; mitigation includes progressive web fallback.
- Regulatory shift (medium) — rules vary by region; mitigation involves legal counsel.
- Merchant adoption (medium) — requires integration density; mitigation via anchor partners.
- Token utility drift (low) — utility decoupling dilutes demand; mitigation via activity-linked rewards.
- Localization quality (low) — weak translations damage trust; mitigation via native review pipeline.

SECTION 9 — Architecture (four layers)
---------------------------------------
- Layer 01 — Client: Telegram Mini App, React + TMA SDK; UI, session, device share, UX state.
- Layer 02 — Edge: auth, Shamir signing orchestration, price feeds, webhooks; stateless functions; holds no share; key reconstructed only transiently on-device during signing.
- Layer 03 — Custody (target architecture): signer service, recovery share registry, Telegram-share binding; hardened environment; planned hardware-backed share protection; holds no single signable key.
- Layer 04 — Settlement: chain adapters, payment processor, indexer, merchant API; TON, EVM, stablecoin rails; idempotent settlement.

SECTION 10 — Growth model
--------------------------
Loops, not campaigns. Referral loop: every active user can refer inside chat with one tap. Merchant loop: accepting ONEWALLET introduces customers to the wallet. Mini-app loop: partner mini-apps require a wallet, driving new sign-ups.

SECTION 11 — Business model
----------------------------
- Swap fee — bps on in-app token swaps; $1 holders pay less. (Designed)
- Merchant fee — bps on settled merchant volume. (Designed)
- Mini-app revenue share — take rate on premium mini-app transactions. (Planned)
- Merchant SaaS — subscription for analytics, refunds, multi-store. (Planned)

SECTION 13 — Glossary
----------------------
- Shamir's Secret Sharing (SSS) — splits a key into N shares so that any K (here 2 of 3) can reconstruct it while fewer than K reveal nothing; ONEWALLET reconstructs the key only briefly, on-device in an isolated context, to sign, then wipes it.
- Threshold scheme (Shamir-based) — a K-of-N access structure; not a threshold signature scheme (TSS), which never reconstructs the key.
- TMA — Telegram Mini App.
- Settlement webhook — a signed HTTP callback used for merchant reconciliation.
- Recovery share — an offline Shamir share used in recovery flows.

Users must not share private wallet, account, or recovery data in any public channel; for account-specific issues, use private support paths only.

SECTION 15 — ONEWALLET AI Assistant
------------------------------------
The website includes the ONEWALLET AI Assistant. It is source-grounded on approved public website, whitepaper, and assistant-corpus material. It can answer questions about wallet setup, Multi-Share (Shamir) security, recovery, payments, fees, $1 utility, roadmap, risks, team, and community channels.

The assistant does not access user accounts, private wallet data, recovery data, or execute wallet actions. Answers can still be wrong and should not be treated as financial, legal, tax, investment, audit, regulatory, exchange-listing, or vendor-architecture advice. If context is unsupported or unsafe, the assistant should fall back to a safe refusal.
